Wilmington for a home seller

Wilmington is Delaware's largest city and the seat of New Castle County, where the Christina River and Brandywine Creek meet before flowing into the Delaware River. It is about 33 miles southwest of Philadelphia. The 2020 count was 70,898 residents, well under the 1940 peak of 112,504, after Interstate 95 cut through neighborhoods in the 1950s and population fell for decades.

The city lists more than 50 named neighborhoods, from Center City, Riverfront and Quaker Hill to Wawaset Park, Brandywine Village and The Flats. It has nine historic districts and one conservation district, Forty Acres. A house inside one of them can face extra review for exterior changes, so ask the city before you start a repair meant to help a sale.

Rowhouses and older construction

Mills and shipyards shaped the street grid, and many Wilmington houses are rowhouses or twins built for the people who worked in them. DuPont began making gunpowder near the Brandywine in 1802, and the neighborhoods that grew up around its mills still show it.

Older construction usually means plaster walls, original wiring, steam or hot water heat and basements that have seen water. Those are the items a buyer's inspector flags first, and they are also what makes a financed sale fall apart late in the process. Get a clear picture of each one before you list, and decide what you will repair, what you will price in and what you will disclose.

The Riverfront is a different case. It was once shipbuilding and manufacturing land and saw state-sponsored renewal beginning in the late 1990s. The 1.2 mile Riverwalk, the convention center and the ballpark anchor a market unlike the older residential blocks inland.

Flood history and your basement

Water is the weather problem that most shapes a Wilmington sale. The remnants of Hurricane Ida flooded hundreds of buildings in September 2021 and displaced dozens of families. The state's floodplain engineer points out that FEMA maps show past risk without allowing for future climate change, and that most homeowners and renters policies leave out flood damage.

  • Look up your parcel's FEMA flood zone before choosing a price or timeline.
  • Pull together insurance claims, repair receipts and drainage work records for the buyer.
  • Expect inspectors to study basements, sump pumps and foundation walls closely.
  • Share what you know, because Delaware's seller disclosure law requires it, as covered below.

Property taxes when you sell

Wilmington bills city property tax, New Castle County sets the assessed value, and the school district adds its own tax. For fiscal year 2026 the city's rates are $3.7413 per $1,000 of assessed value for residential property and $5.8276 per $1,000 for non-residential property. The city said these raise the same total revenue as the year before, and that its figures rest on the county's first countywide reassessment since 1983.

City bills go out in July with the city portion due September 30. County and school taxes come due November 30. Rates can change from one year to the next, so read the current bill on the city's property tax page before you do any math.

A senior exemption covers the first $210,300 of assessed value. Income limits apply, and applications are due May 16.

Taxes are normally prorated at settlement. If you have not paid the current bill, it is usually taken out of your proceeds.

Transfer tax and closing steps

Expect a realty transfer tax of 4 percent of value in most sales, split into 2.5 percent for the state and 1.5 percent for the county or municipality, and shared equally by the seller and buyer under the statute. Wilmington adds its own transfer tax rules in Chapter 44, Article IV of the city code.

On the city's exemption affidavit you will find foreclosure, divorce, mortgage default, governmental transfers and parent and child. Its first-time buyer exemption applies only if the buyer has had no legal interest in residential real estate in Wilmington for at least three years and plans to move in within 90 days.

  • An attorney has to run the settlement. The Delaware Supreme Court's 2000 Mid-Atlantic Settlement Services decision and a September 22, 2006 order treat closings as practicing law.
  • Under 30 Del. C. 5402, the first-time buyer's portion can shrink by 0.5 percent of the first $400,000, up to $2,000. What the seller owes does not change.
  • A nonresident individual seller sends estimated tax on the gain, at 6.6 percent, with Form REW EST when the deed is presented for recording.

Rental licenses and vacant property fees

Rental owners hold a Residential Property Rental License that renews yearly under city code section 5-92. A rental you have just acquired gets registered with the Department of Licenses and Inspections, and either side of a sale may be asked to show proof of it. Inspections come every two or five years, depending on how many units there are.

Empty houses cost money here. If you inherited a property or the last tenant moved out, the vacant property fee climbs with each year of vacancy, and a change of owner does not reset it:

Years vacantAnnual fee
Less than 1$0
1$500
2$1,000
3 to 4$2,000
5 to 9$3,500
10$5,000, plus $500 for each year after

The department must hear from you within 30 days of a sale or a mailing address change. Skipping registration can draw a fine of up to $500 or a civil action. Request a payoff figure from the city early so closing day brings no surprise.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Wilmington houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What a Wilmington seller must disclose

State law makes you write down every material defect you know of before a buyer makes an offer on a house with up to four units. The form is the Seller's Disclosure of Real Property Condition Report, and the rule comes from the Buyer Property Protection Act. Section 2572 sets the timing at before the listing agreement is signed, and requires you to update the buyer if something material changes ahead of settlement.

Section 2577 lists transfers that are exempt: court-ordered ones involving an estate, trust or guardianship, deeds in lieu of foreclosure, sheriff's sales, and transfers among co-owners or to a spouse or lineal relative. Selling as an executor, or after a foreclosure filing? Your attorney can tell you which category applies.

Cash sale or listing?

Choosing between a cash buyer and a listing comes down to speed against exposure. With cash there is no lender, so no loan approval or appraisal, and closing can follow your calendar once title is clear. A listing reaches more buyers, but it brings showings, repair requests and the risk that a buyer's financing collapses.

Both routes still go through an attorney's closing, the transfer tax split and payoff of any city charges. We purchase houses as-is and name no price until we have seen the property. Decline an offer and you owe nothing.

To compare fairly, put together the deed, your latest tax bill, any rental license, flood or repair records, and a written list of what you know about the house. Then a cash offer and a listing price can be weighed on the same terms.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the realty transfer tax when selling a house in Wilmington?

It is normally 4 percent of the property value, with 2.5 percent going to the state and 1.5 percent to the local government, and Delaware law divides it equally between seller and buyer. Wilmington has its own transfer tax rules in Chapter 44, Article IV of the city code, so confirm your exact figure with your closing attorney.

Do I need an attorney to sell my house in Wilmington?

Yes. Delaware requires an attorney to conduct real estate settlements, following the Delaware Supreme Court's 2000 Mid-Atlantic Settlement Services decision and its September 22, 2006 order.

When are Wilmington city property taxes due?

City bills go out in July, with the city payment due September 30 and county and school taxes due November 30. Check the city's property tax page for the current year's dates.

What happens if my Wilmington house has been empty for years?

The city charges a vacant property fee that grows with each year of vacancy, from $0 under one year to $5,000 at ten years, plus $500 for each extra year. The fee follows the property, so it continues even if ownership changes.

Can I sell a Wilmington house that has flood damage?

Yes, but you must disclose known material defects in writing under 6 Del. C. 2572. Gather repair records and insurance claims, since most homeowners policies do not cover flood damage.

Dover in brief

Dover is Delaware's capital and the seat of Kent County, and after Wilmington it is the state's second-largest city. State government is the biggest employer, Kent County government is another large one, and Dover Air Force Base in the southeast corner of the city anchors the rest of the local economy. Military orders arrive on a schedule that owners do not control, so some Dover sellers need to close fast once a move is ordered.

The city is flat and spread out along a handful of roads. US 13 is the Dupont Highway commercial strip, US 13 Alternate crosses downtown on Governors Avenue, DE 1 is a toll road east of town toward Wilmington and the beaches, DE 8 follows Division Street, and DE 15 serves the west side. Buyers who commute care about the distance to those roads more than about a neighborhood label.

Older houses near the Green

William Penn founded Dover in 1683 as a court town, and the Green still holds the Kent County Courthouse and the Delaware Supreme Court. Twenty sites in the city are on the National Register of Historic Places, among them the Dover Green and Victorian Dover historic districts.

Owners of older houses downtown can run into design review for exterior work, and the city publishes guidelines for its historic districts. If your house is near the Green, call the planning office before you pay for a repair, so you learn whether it needs approval first.

Roof, flood and storm records

Dover sits along the St. Jones River, and wind is a real concern here: a tornado tied to Tropical Storm Isaias in August 2020 caused damage in the city. A buyer or insurer will ask what you know about the roof and the drainage around the house, so put the answers on paper before you list.

  • Write down the age of the roof and any storm repairs.
  • Look up your parcel on the city's floodplain management page.
  • Gather receipts for HVAC replacement or service.
  • Photograph siding and any trees close to the house.

None of this changes what the house is worth, but a folder of records shortens the back and forth with an inspector.

Two property tax bills

A Dover owner pays tax twice, once to the city and once through Kent County, and the two follow separate calendars. The city rate is $0.485 per $100 of assessed value, applied to values set at 100 percent of January 1, 2020 fair market value. The city revalues every five years, most recently in 2020. City bills go out July 1, with supplemental bills in the first week of October, January and April.

Kent County's tax year runs June 1 to May 31. Its last reassessment took effect July 1, 2023. Bills usually reach owners by mid-August, and the full annual amount is due by September 30. Selling a house does not trigger a reassessment.

Reach the city tax office at 302-736-7005. The county assessment office is at 555 Bay Road, Dover, phone 302-744-2401.

Disputing the city assessment

Each April 1 the city puts its assessment register on display. Appeals are due April 30 by 5:00 p.m., and the city does not honor postmarks, so a letter sent on the final day arrives too late. Deliver it by hand or mail it well ahead.

Start by checking the record against the house itself: square footage, bathrooms, a finished basement, outbuildings. Factual errors are the simplest appeals to win. The county bill has its own January 31 window for annual assessments, and the county assessment office can walk you through it.

Transfer tax and recording a deed

Delaware charges a realty transfer tax that normally adds up to 4 percent: 2.5 percent to the state and 1.5 percent to the local government. By default buyer and seller each pay half, though a contract can shift that. First-time homebuyers can trim their half by 0.5 percent of up to $400,000, worth at most $2,000.

The Kent County Recorder of Deeds, at 555 Bay Road, records Dover deeds. Nothing goes on record until fees and taxes are paid, and a form with mistakes can cost a $40 nonconforming fee or a $20 rejection fee. Because an attorney must conduct the settlement in Delaware, that attorney ordinarily takes care of the filing.

An ordinance covering unincorporated areas sets a 1.5 percent transfer tax, but Dover is a city. Have your attorney confirm which local tax reaches a property inside the city.

Rental permits and vacant buildings

A rental house in Dover needs an annual rental dwelling permit, which expires every January 31, and an owner who lives outside Kent County has to name a property manager based in the county. Settle the permit and any fees before the closing date.

Rentals of less than 30 days face limits. The 2021 ordinance says the owner must live in Dover and may only offer a primary residence, and the annual license is void once ownership transfers.

  • Under the vacant building article, a building counts as vacant after more than three consecutive months without occupants.
  • The owner registers within 30 days of the building going vacant and reports changes within 30 days.
  • Unpaid fees can land on the tax bill, and the city can insist on payment before title moves.

The planning office can confirm the latest wording and fees.

What Delaware requires you to disclose

Before a buyer can make an offer on a one to four unit home, Delaware wants a completed Seller's Disclosure of Real Property Condition Report, a written statement of every material defect you know about. Section 2577 carves out some transfers: estate, trust and guardianship transfers, deeds in lieu of foreclosure, sheriff's sales, and transfers among relatives.

Selling to us as-is means no repair list. You still complete the disclosure, and the attorney still runs the closing.

Steps from decision to closing

Most Dover sales, cash or financed, move through the same sequence:

  1. Choose a closing attorney first, because Delaware requires one to run the settlement.
  2. Collect the deed and your newest city and county tax bills.
  3. Phone the city tax office for a balance, and the planning office if the property is a rental or has stood vacant.
  4. Fill in the disclosure report truthfully and keep a copy for yourself.
  5. Get the closing date and the transfer tax split into the written agreement.

Paying cash removes the appraisal and loan approval, so closing can follow as soon as title work and the attorney's settlement are ready. A financed buyer needs both of those first.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a house sale take in Dover, Delaware?

It depends on the route. A cash sale can close as soon as the title work and the attorney settlement are ready, while a financed sale also needs appraisal and loan approval. Delaware requires an attorney to conduct the settlement either way.

When are Dover city property tax bills due?

Dover mails city tax bills on July 1, with supplemental bills in the first week of October, January and April. Kent County bills usually arrive by mid-August, and the annual tax is due by September 30.

Where are deeds recorded for a Dover house?

Deeds are recorded with the Kent County Recorder of Deeds at 555 Bay Road in Dover. The office will not record a deed until the correct fees and taxes are collected.

Do I have to disclose problems when selling my Dover house?

Yes, unless the sale is exempt. Delaware's Buyer Property Protection Act calls for a written disclosure of known material defects, with exemptions for court-ordered transfers, foreclosure sales and certain family transfers.

Does Dover Air Force Base affect selling a house here?

It can. Military orders move on a schedule, so some owners must sell on short notice, and a cash sale can fit that kind of deadline.

What sets the Newark market apart

Newark is in New Castle County, about 8 miles west-southwest of Wilmington and 28 miles southwest of Philadelphia, just east of the Maryland line. The 2020 Census counted 30,601 residents with a median age of 24.2. That low number reflects the University of Delaware, whose campus sits beside Main Street, the commercial center.

For a seller, the student population is the main fact about the local housing market. It creates steady rental demand, and it also brings a set of city rules that decide what a house can be used for after you sell it.

Location, rail and roads

I-95 and Delaware routes 2, 72, 273, 279 and 896 all serve Newark. The Newark rail station is on the Northeast Corridor with SEPTA and Amtrak service, and DART First State and DART Connect buses use the Newark Transit Hub.

Rail access draws commuters and students who live without a car. Houses within walking distance of the station or Main Street tend to attract a different crowd than houses on the outskirts, so describe where yours sits and let buyers decide what that is worth to them.

Rental permits and student homes

An annual rental permit is required for non-owner-occupied property leased to tenants, and also for an owner-occupied home that rents rooms to more than two unrelated people. A change of ownership, even between relatives, calls for an updated rental license application.

Student homes get the most specific treatment. The city defines one as a single-family detached dwelling occupied by three post-secondary students who are unrelated by blood or adoption, and it sets these conditions:

  • No more than three people may live in a student home.
  • It must sit farther from any other student home than ten times the required lot width for a single-family house in that district.
  • Rentals that already held permits when the ordinance was adopted count toward that distance.
  • Thirty-three listed subdivisions and some listed streets are outside the definition.

Zoning limits non-owner-occupied single-family rentals to three unrelated occupants in the RH, RT, RS, RD and RR districts, and four in RM. Some deeds set lower limits, so read yours. An investor who wants to keep renting your house, particularly as a student home, has to check the distance rule before making an offer.

Inspection and exterior rules for rentals

The Code Enforcement Division requires exterior and common-area inspections for rentals, and rental units get an annual inspection. Ask the division which inspections apply to your unit, since interior visits are described as voluntary in some places and required in others.

The city lists these upkeep rules for rental properties:

  • Refuse cans of 20 or 32 gallons, labeled with the address, with tight lids.
  • Curbside refuse under 40 pounds, set out no earlier than 6:00 p.m. the day before collection.
  • Weed and grass notices once growth passes 10 inches.
  • Snow and ice cleared from the sidewalk within 24 hours, leaving a path at least three feet wide.

Leases longer than 30 days are required, and an occupant posting must hang inside the unit. Code Enforcement is at 220 South Main Street, phone (302) 366-7000.

Newark property taxes

The city real estate tax rate for 2026 to 2027 is $0.2464 per $100 of assessed value. Bills are issued after July 1 and are due by September 30 to avoid a penalty. New Castle County's Assessment Office sets the assessed value, which drives both the city tax and the school tax, and assessments are listed as of April 1.

Utilities and the closing statement

Newark runs its own electric department, serving about 12,800 customers, and a water system serving about 33,000. Because the city is the utility, a final meter reading and a payoff figure matter at settlement. Ask for both a few days before closing so nothing is left on your account when the deed is recorded.

Delaware's realty transfer tax is normally 4 percent, made up of 2.5 percent for the state and 1.5 percent for the county or municipality. The law divides it equally between seller and buyer. We buy Newark houses as-is, including houses with rental history. Offers are not promised until we see the property.

What to have ready

Collect your deed, the latest city tax bill, the county assessed value, your final utility figures and the completed disclosure report. Choose the closing attorney early, because the attorney opens the title search and will ask for these papers first. If the house is a rental, add the permit, the last inspection result and the lease. Having everything in one folder lets a buyer make a firm offer faster and cuts down on questions in the last week before closing.

Selling a house with tenants or rental history

A sale of a rented house raises questions an owner-occupied sale does not. Sort these out before you accept a closing date.

  • Confirm whether your rental permit is current and ask Code Enforcement at (302) 366-7000 about the discontinuation form if the rental is ending.
  • Find out what the lease says about notice and showings, and give tenants written notice for each visit.
  • Tell the buyer whether the house has been used as a student home, since that status affects what they can do with it.
  • Keep copies of the last passed inspection and any notices from the city.

A cash buyer who wants a vacant house will usually ask when the tenants leave, so a clear move-out date helps. If a buyer plans to keep renting, the updated rental license application must be filed after the ownership change.

You need a valid permit while the house is rented, and any ownership change calls for an updated rental license application, even between related parties. Contact Code Enforcement at (302) 366-7000 for the discontinuation form if the rental ends.

What is a student home in Newark?

It is a single-family detached dwelling occupied by three post-secondary students unrelated by blood or adoption. A student home must meet a distance requirement from other student homes and may have no more than three occupants.

When is Newark city property tax due?

Bills are issued after July 1 and must be paid by September 30 to avoid a penalty. For 2026 to 2027 the city rate is $0.2464 per $100 of assessed value.

New Castle County's Assessment Office sets them, and the Board of Assessment Review decides appeals. Call the county at (302) 395-5520 for appeal forms.

Middletown's housing market

Middletown, in southern New Castle County, was incorporated in 1861. Its population went from 6,161 in 2000 to 18,871 in 2010 and reached 23,192 in the 2020 Census, helped along by land annexations. Most of the housing around the old center is recent subdivision construction, so a resale house competes with new homes from builders as well as with other resales.

The historic blocks are small by comparison. Anyone who is selling there should expect buyers to compare the house against newer neighbors on size, systems and finishes, and should be ready to explain what has been updated.

Getting around from Middletown

Two toll roads bracket the town. DE 1 runs along the east edge with an exit at Odessa for DE 299, and US 301 lies just west and north with exits for DE 299 and DE 71. Inside town, DE 71 follows Broad Street and DE 299 follows Main Street. DART First State buses serve Routes 46, 37 and 302, and there is no passenger rail.

Describe highway access as it is. Buyers who commute north toward Wilmington or south toward Dover will check the drive themselves, and an honest description saves a wasted showing. National retail and food chains have grown along the US 301 corridor.

Town utilities at closing

Middletown runs its own Electric Department and Water/Wastewater Department, and an Amazon fulfillment center and a ChristianaCare emergency department are among the larger local operations. For a seller, the utility side is the part that shows up on the settlement statement.

New accounts for the buyer are set up through the settlement attorneys, so nobody has to visit Town Hall. A late fee of 6 percent applies once a utility bill is seven days past due, so clear your final bills before the closing date.

  • Pay the last electric, water, sewer and trash bills before settlement.
  • Ask your attorney to request a tax and utility payoff figure from the town.
  • Keep your account number and online payment PIN handy for the final bill.

Which school district serves Middletown?

The Appoquinimink School District covers Middletown. It formed when Middletown School District 60 and Odessa School District 61 merged on July 1, 1969. Its high schools include Middletown High School, Appoquinimink High School (opened 2008) and Odessa High School (opened 2020).

Families usually ask about school boundaries first, so find out which school your address feeds before you list and have the answer ready.

Property taxes in Middletown

The town bills its own property tax from New Castle County's assessed value, while the county and the school district send separate bills. Town bills go out around August 1 and must reach the Town Tax Office by September 30 to avoid penalties. Each month a bill sits overdue adds a 1.5 percent penalty.

Seniors 65 and older who have lived in town for at least a year can apply once for a discount. The application is due before July 1 for that tax year. The discount stays with the residence, so a new owner has to apply again.

New Castle County reassessed every property in 2025, the first countywide reassessment since 1983. Your assessed value may therefore look nothing like what the previous owner paid. Look yours up on the county parcel search before you set price expectations, and call the Tax Office for the current town rate.

Selling a Middletown rental

Rental owners register with the town, and the unit is inspected at every change of tenant. The first inspection costs $75, one re-inspection is free, and the unit must be vacant and clean. Registration is renewed every three years from approval. Anyone who owns two or more rental units, and any authorized agent, needs a town business license.

Under the town's Clean Hands Ordinance, past-due bills and fees on the property must be paid before an inspection is scheduled. A tenant who wants utility service needs a passed town inspection and a $300 deposit, and only electric and trash can be in the tenant's name. Water and sewer stay with the owner.

  • A mobile home buyer cannot set up service until the previous owner's taxes are paid in full.
  • Tell the town in writing when rental information changes.
  • Ask the town how ownership transfers are handled for registered rentals.

Paperwork to gather before asking for offers

Missing paperwork slows a Delaware closing more than anything about the house itself. If these items are ready, a cash buyer or a listing agent can move quickly.

  • Your deed and the name of the closing attorney you plan to use.
  • The latest town tax bill and the assessed value from the county parcel search.
  • Final readings and balances for electric, water, sewer and trash, all billed by the town.
  • The Seller's Disclosure of Real Property Condition Report, filled out honestly, with radon information if you have any.
  • For a rental, the town registration, the last passed inspection and any tenant notices.

If you inherited the house, an exemption for transfers by a fiduciary may apply to the disclosure duty, and your attorney can confirm. A completed disclosure form shows good faith. It is not a warranty and does not replace the buyer's own inspection.

From first offer to closing day

Whether the buyer pays cash or uses a loan, the sequence is similar. You agree on terms, a closing attorney opens the title work, and any open tax or utility balance is found and listed for payoff. Then the buyer's side reviews the disclosure report and, if there is a loan, the lender orders an appraisal. On closing day the attorney collects signatures, records the deed and sends your proceeds after paying off whatever is owed.

A cash buyer skips the appraisal and loan approval, which are the steps that most often shift a closing date. Before you agree to a date, make sure your final utility readings and tax payoff can be ready by then. Ask for the agreement in writing, and read who pays which closing cost before you sign.

Transfer tax and settlement rules

Delaware's usual realty transfer tax is 4 percent: 2.5 percent for the state and 1.5 percent for the county or municipality. The statute splits it equally between seller and buyer. A first-time homebuyer can reduce the buyer's share by 0.5 percent of up to $400,000, with a ceiling of $2,000.

An attorney must conduct the settlement, and a seller of a one to four unit home must hand over the Seller's Disclosure of Real Property Condition Report before an offer. Nonresident individual sellers pay estimated tax of 6.6 percent of the gain, with Form REW EST, when the deed is recorded.

Frequently asked questions

When are Middletown property taxes due?

The Town of Middletown mails bills around August 1, and they must reach the Tax Office by September 30 to avoid penalties. A 1.5 percent penalty applies for each month a bill is overdue.

Who sets my assessed value in Middletown?

New Castle County sets it, and the town applies its rate to that figure. The county finished a countywide reassessment in 2025, the first since 1983.

Do I need to inspect a Middletown rental before tenants move out or in?

Yes. The town requires an inspection at each change of tenant, with a $75 first inspection fee and one free re-inspection. Past-due bills at the property must be paid before scheduling.

How do utilities transfer when I sell a Middletown house?

Account setup for the buyer goes through the settlement attorneys. As the seller, pay your final bills first, because a 6 percent late charge applies once a bill is seven days past due.

Which school district is Middletown in?

The Appoquinimink School District serves Middletown, with Middletown High School, Appoquinimink High School and Odessa High School among its high schools.
